frame: An opinion piece in the Bluster Rock Bugle is about a new marine sanctuary. Wren has circled it twice.
text: SAVE CORAL GULLY, by marine scientist Dr Lena Moss. Coral Gully, on the northern side of Bluster Rock, is home to the island's last healthy patch of reef. In the past five years, our surveys have found that the number of fish on the reef has fallen by almost half, and the giant clams that once lined the gully have nearly disappeared. I believe the council should make Coral Gully a no-fishing sanctuary, where the reef can rest and recover. Some fishing families fear the sanctuary will leave their nets empty, but at Pelican Point, catches just outside a sanctuary doubled within ten years. That happens because fish grow large and breed inside the protected area, then spill out into the surrounding water. Healthy reefs also attract snorkellers, who spend money in local cafes, dive shops and caravan parks. Some people say the council cannot afford new signs and patrol boats. The decision will be made at the council meeting on the first Monday of next month, and I urge every resident who cares about the reef to come along and speak up. Children are welcome too, and the surf club will run a free sausage sizzle afterwards. Copies of our survey results are available at the library.

frame: The Countaby found an article about the ghost tours at the old Bluster Rock cemetery.
text:
KEEP THE LANTERN TOURS, by Ezra Finch, tour guide. For twelve years, the Lantern Tours have led visitors through the old Bluster Rock cemetery after dark, telling the true stories of the miners, cooks and camel drivers who built this town. Each tour raises money to repair the crumbling headstones, and last year we fixed thirty-one of them. Visitors come from all over the country, and many are descendants of the people buried there, hoping to learn more about their own families. Without the tours, these stories would be forgotten, and the headstones would keep falling apart.

Some neighbours have complained that the tours are noisy, and that torch beams shine through their bedroom windows late at night. They are right, and I am sorry. From next month, every tour will finish by half past eight, and our guides will use red lanterns, which are far dimmer than torches. We will also stay on the paths at the far end, well away from the houses.

The Lantern Tours bring history to life in a way no textbook can. Last month, a Year 5 class joined a tour and wrote a whole book about the camel drivers. Our guides are all volunteers, and they would be heartbroken to stop. I hope the council will let them continue.
